html:
The Parthian Empire was an Iranian empire that ruled Iran and Mesopotamia from 247 BCE to 224 CE, and for nearly three centuries was Rome's great rival in the east. It is also called the Arsacid Empire, after its founder, Arsaces I.

Arsaces led the Parni, a nomad people from the steppe, into the province of Parthia in north-east Iran, then held by the Seleucid Empire. Under Mithridates I, in the second century BCE, the Parthians took Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids. Their winter capital became Ctesiphon on the Tigris.

The empire sat across the trade routes between the Mediterranean and China, just as the Silk Road opened. Parthian merchants carried Chinese silk west and grew rich as middlemen.

Their army was built on horsemen: armoured lancers and mounted archers who could shoot backward while riding away, the "Parthian shot". It gave Rome some of its worst defeats:

  • In 53 BCE at the Battle of Carrhae the Parthians destroyed the army of the Roman general Crassus.
  • For two centuries the two empires fought over Armenia and northern Mesopotamia. The Roman emperor Trajan took Ctesiphon in 116 CE, but Rome could not hold it.

The state was loose. Great noble families and vassal kings held much of the land. Early kings used Greek on their coins and called themselves "friends of the Greeks"; later ones leaned more on Iranian traditions, and tolerated many religions, including Zoroastrianism. In 224 CE Ardashir I, a vassal king in Persis, overthrew the last Parthian king and founded the Sasanian Empire.
